sentences.asr: While the size of Arctic sea ice has dropped by about 40% over 40 years, until recently, the size of the sea ice around Antarctica was slowly increasing.
Then, after 2015, Antarctic ice extent fell from a record high to several record lows, losing an area as large as Greenland.
Some research has suggested that higher air temperatures may be the cause.
However, two new studies show that ocean warming played a bigger role in this dramatic change.
As part of global ocean circulation, warm saltwater moves southward from the tropics and circles Antarctica 200 meters below the surface.
But temperature and saltiness records of the past 20 years suggest that this warm, deep saltwater has been rising towards the surface, where it can melt sea ice.
Antarctica is encircled by a belt of strong winds and storms.
Climate change has pushed this storm belt southward, bringing more rain and snow into the sea ice area, according to a study by Earl Wilson and other researchers at Stanford University.
The rain and snow create a layer of fresh surface water that better protects the bottom of the sea ice from warm deep saltwater, allowing it to grow to its 2014 record high.
But the same southward moving storm belt also brings stronger winds.
These winds blow surface water and ice forward.
As this happens, warm deep saltwater rises up to fill the empty space.
Between 2014 and 2016, this wind-driven rising began to get the upper hand against the protective layer of increased rain and snow, and sea ice began to melt away.
When the researchers input the recorded ocean data into a computer model, it projected that sea ice would grow and then become smaller, as it did in the real world.
The researchers plan to study and model other things, which also likely play roles throughout Antarctica.
Examples include changes in sea ice movement and increases in ocean mixing resulting from more storms.
By studying the ocean data, they hope to build a model to project changes in Antarctic sea ice in the years to come.
The internet has provided us with unmatched ways to get information, but it is also sounding alarms.
Some experts argue that the internet will produce forgetfulness in the minds of those learning to use it because they won't practice their memory.
Is the internet really doing harm to our memories? Or will our doubtful experts be proven wrong?
After all, the brain's attention system and preferences for novel experiences were already there long before the digital age, and our ability to remember is nearly inexhaustible.
According to Michael Mirzenisch, a brain researcher, every brain is a work in progress. It keeps changing throughout our lives, depending on how we use it.
But our brains don't work well when we're not focused.
When we repeatedly check text messages and social media during work, we are weakening our ability to form both short and long-term memories. Experts say,
The flood of information influences our ability to remember too.
Though our brains are designed to look for new data, too much of it may be causing this natural drive to go wild.
The compulsion to continuously take in information means we often check social media when we should be doing memory housekeeping by giving our brains some rest.
Another problem, the effortless way of receiving information online.
Trying to actively recall data is a good workout for the brain, but today we are using online search tools instead.
However, the internet may be changing only what we remember, not our ability to do so, suggests Columbia University psychologist Betsy Sparrow.
In fact, the internet is becoming an outside hard drive for our memories.
Some worry that this is having a negative effect on society, but Sparrow suggests this will change our way of learning from a focus on remembering facts to one on understanding ideas.
As is shown in a 2008 study, using the internet exercised the brain more than reading among older adults with strong computer skills.
And two Harvard psychologists argue that not needing to remember facts might free our minds to focus on more meaningful tasks.
There may be costs caused by our increased dependence on the internet. But generally, the benefits are going to outweigh those costs, says Benjamin Storm, a psychologist.
It seems pretty clear that memory is changing, but is it changing for the better?
At this point, we don't know.
A Chinese robot became the unexpected star in an international kite festival.
At the beginning of the festival, the robot held the string of a kite flying in the sky and made up and down movements.
The show lasted for 20 minutes and drew crowds of visitors to take photos.
The robot in the International Festival is a good example of human-like robots.
In recent years, human-like running robots have greatly improved and surprised the world.
This year, a robot from a Chinese company broke the men's record for the half marathon.
In another event, a robot, also from a Chinese company, came close to the men's 100-meter world record.
Robots are not just for flying a kite or running in competitions.
They are also helping on farms.
Picking tomatoes is tiring work for humans.
Now farming robots can help with it.
The robots first get information about the tomatoes on their own.
The information is about whether the tomatoes are ripe or not, and whether there are any tomatoes hidden behind leaves.
With the information, the robots can work out the most effective way to pick the fruit.
When picking tomatoes, the robots must choose ripe tomatoes and leave unripe ones untouched.
There are many reasons for the rapid improvement of robots in recent years.
The cost of building robots has fallen a lot.
New computer chips allow machines to perform better.
With the development of technology, robots are playing an increasingly important role in everyday life.
Scientists have studied animals' feelings for hundreds of years.
However, the past research mainly focused on animals' negative feelings, such as pain and fear.
This can help reduce animals' suffering, but it doesn't tell what brings them happiness.
Now some scientists are working together to better understand animals' joy.
They are trying to measure joy in animals in a new study.
The scientists define joy as a strong positive feeling which is caused by an event, such as seeing a friend or a favorite food.
They have created a set of ways to measure the feeling in different animals.
The scientists want to make sure that the final result is not from just guessing animals' minds, but from scientific research.
Some signs of joy are connected with actions.
For example, some scientists have noticed that chimpanzees make laugh-like sounds while they are playing.
Other scientists have noticed that dolphins produce joyful sounds when happy things happen to them.
However, actions do not tell the whole story.
Horses seem to be happily playing, but they may actually have the opposite feeling. They are downcast.
So the scientists are also examining animals' brain chemistry and studying their body temperature changes to help tell if the animals are truly happy.
Learning about joy in animals can improve the care of animals.
And the new study about animals' happiness can also help us better understand humans' happiness.
Packing for a family holiday often feels like a rush to remember necessary things like socks or medicine.
However, for children, packing can be valuable because it helps them learn math in real life.
Counting is a basic math skill.
Before they pack, children should first think about the activities in the holiday.
Different activities require different things.
Then they will count the days of the trip, and how many things they will take.
For example, if swimming is included, they may need to take swimming clothes.
If the trip lasts seven days, they will consider how many clothes they need.
In this process, they practice counting.
Sometimes, the suitcase is not big enough.
After they fail to pack everything in, children quickly learn the importance of space.
They might try folding their clothes in different ways to make them smaller.
By trying again and again, children start to understand something like volume.
More importantly, the questions from adults can guide children toward deep thinking.
For example, when the mother sees her child put milk and clothes together, she may ask her child if it is okay to do so.
The child has to consider whether it is proper to pack that way.
If not, the child will think about what the proper way is.
Deep thinking is what children need when they solve difficult math problems.
Learning math happens not only at a desk, but also in other places.
Therefore, when parents do housework, children should try to take part if possible.
Io Mingpei was known as the master of modern architecture.
He designed many famous buildings and landmarks around the world.
Pei was born in Guangzhou in 1917.
He grew up in a family that valued education and traditional art.
Suzhou was his ancestral hometown.
Pei spent most of his childhood holidays there.
During those holidays, he would visit the gardens whenever he had time.
Seeing those rocks, stone bridges and waterfalls, he began to show interest in them.
At the age of 10, Pei moved with his family to Shanghai.
The city's international architectural style had a strong influence on him.
He decided to become an architect.
In 1935, Pei went abroad to study.
When he was thirty eight, he started his company in New York.
In 1983, he won the Pritzker Prize, the highest honor in architecture.
One of Pay's most famous works is the Glass Pyramid in front of the Louvre Museum in Paris.
It was completed in 1989.
It showed his idea. Let Light design the buildings.
Many people disliked it because it was so different from the traditional architecture at that time.
But today, it is one of the most popular places in France.
Suzhou Museum is another work of his.
It opened in 2006, and became a must-see place later.
Pei explained. It should belong to Suzhou, but also to the world.
It should be traditional, yet moderned.
He created over 50 designs during his life.
Pei passed away in 2019, at the age of 102.
His designs are regarded as gifts to the world.
Last summer, we visited a bank in Kunmang, but this bank holds life instead of money.
It's called the germplasm bank of wild species in southwest China.
Its seed bank, the largest one in Asia, keeps nearly 100,000 collections from over 11,000 kinds of wild plants.
We learned that many scientists made hard journeys to fill this bank.
They climbed mountains, crossed highlands, and traveled through forests to collect valuable seeds.
One scientist, Li Hangs, led more than 20 trips to high mountains, even after the age of 61, and got badly hurt after falling from the back of a horse during her work.
But nothing could stop her.
She often said to her team, choose one thing and give yourself to it.
Another scientist, Gyo Yanji, collected seeds from Mount Chomolangma at 6,212 meters above sea level.
This is the highest place ever for collecting plant seeds.
He spent over 200 days, a year in the wild, just to add one more kind of plant seed to the bank.
A seed is hope one scientist shared.
These seeds are not just tiny plant parts. They carry genes that may help us grow better crops, make new medicines, or bring back lost forests.
But some kinds of plants are disappearing, and we may lose them forever.
Therefore, collecting valuable seeds is a race against time.
It is a job that needs patience, courage, and love.
Saving seeds is everyone's job.
Such seed banks are not only found in China.
By working with seed banks in Norway, the UK, and some other countries around the world, the scientists can turn these treasures into a shared hope for the far future.
As we left, we had a deeper respect for the scientists who have spent their lives on this quiet but great work.
The seeds they save carry life, hope, and a better future for all living things on the earth.
Ai is a 22-year-old girl from Kashkir, Xinjiang.
She became well known in a new season of a TV program, which tells people how young people build their careers after leaving school.
The program followed 12 students who studied traditional Chinese medicine, TCM.
As the youngest one, I at first was unnoticed.
By the end of the season, however, she surprised all with her great progress.
Ai was not from a family of doctors.
Her earliest interest in traditional medicine was awakened in her old town.
In that place, people believed mutton soup cured illness faster than seeing doctors in hospital.
When her grandmother died of illness, she realized good doctors were needed in that place.
That was when she decided to become one to serve the people there.
In 2018, thanks to an education program for Xinjiang middle school students, I had a chance to study in a Shenzhen high school.
Three years later, she was accepted by Guangzhou University of Chinese Medicine.
However, the road to becoming a TCM doctor was never easy.
For her, it was especially difficult to understand ancient Chinese medical books.
Terms like yin and yang were a totally new way of thinking.
So I was always half a step behind my classmates Ai said.
To catch up, she put in more time and developed a study method of her own.
Along with her schoolwork, IE got practical experience by taking part in more than 13 volunteer activities.
Ai's greatest dream is to return to Xinjiang and use her TCM knowledge to serve local people.
Back in Kashgar, I know many people don't look for medical care, so I believe it's deeply meaningful to use TCM, which is simple and cheap and works well IE said.
Motorcycle helmets are important.
They protect riders from getting hurt.
In 2017, about 1,872 riders in the US were saved because of helmet use.
Effective helmets do more than protect people in accidents.
They also help keep wind and small flying pieces off riders' faces.
Before the 1970s, motorcycle helmets were made of plastic, offering little protection.
Today, they are made of carbon fiber, much lighter and stronger than before.
Now they are safer and more comfortable.
With the development of technology, modern helmets are smarter.
Through Bluetooth connected speakers, riders can make telephone calls as they travel along the road.
Cameras are also found in modern helmets.
They can record what is happening ahead, like the cameras in cars. And they are easy to control by voice.
The visors in certain helmets are able to change their color.
They become dark when the sun shines too brightly, or when strong light from cars and trucks hits riders' faces.
In this way, writers can avoid strong light and see better.
These days, AI is changing people's way of life.
For motorcycle riders, AI can now be placed inside helmets to achieve greater safety.
One such example is the ICR Smart Helmet.
This helmet can show the objects around the motorcycle.
The riders don't need to turn their heads or take their eyes off the road ahead to get a better sense of the road situation.
The helmet can also receive all the important information, such as speed, direction and traffic accidents.
When a rider decides where to go, the helmet shows different ways to get there on the inside of the visor.
It can even warn the rider when necessary, like when a motorcycle gets too close to a car.
Ms. Beryl and Layla are great friends.
It doesn't matter that Beryl is 87 and Layla is 4.
The pair have many interests in common, and they spend a lot of time together.
They make drawings, play games, and laugh at each other's jokes.
The two attend an intergenerational preschool called Mother Nurture.
It brings society's oldest and youngest members together in a community.
At Mother Nurture the kids have someone who can tell great stories, but who also has the time and patience to really listen to them, says director Penny Livingston.
Many of the children do not have grandparents in the same city, and their friendships with their elderly classmates make it possible for them to get along with people at a different stage of life.
For the elderly, the experience is also rewarding.
The children bring the joy and excitement of youth into their lives, and the time spent with kids improves their health.
The elderly report feeling less lonely.
Their minds work better, and even their bodies seem to benefit from staying with the children because they move more.
Mother Nurture is just one of many such programs that have appeared around the world.
The programs work, and even the kids' parents benefit.
Many families do not have relatives nearby, and the chance for their children to spend time with a person like a grandmother or grandfather pleases parents.
We kind of get stuck with people who are the same age as a Sesmaya, a caregiver who has worked at Mother Nurture for three years.
When I see how careful the children are around their older friends, I know they are developing empathy for people who are different, she says.
And that is good news for the rest of us, since we will all be old one day.
